QuEra、哈佛大学和Anthropic研究表明，利用
AI
可
减少量子电路资源需求
11月10日，QuEra、哈佛大学和Anthropic的研究人员利用Claude设计了量子电路，能够在七到八个计算构建模块中减少门数和量子比特需求。研究表明，Reed-Solomon解码器的Toffoli门减少了12倍，库仑势计算中总资源减少了9.9倍，定点高斯函数减少了39倍。团队还开发了一种新的可逆模块反演方法，在门数和量子比特需求之间提供了额外的权衡。

IBM宣布Nighthawk r3，计划2027年推出1040量子比特系统
11月
11日，IBM宣布下一代Quantum Nighthawk r3处理器，设计用于在520个可编程量子比特上执行10000次量子运算，计划于2027年将两个处理器连接成1040量子比特的系统。当前的Nighthawk r2处理器支持120个量子比特上的7500多次量子操作，每秒可达10万个采样，IBM报告称在多个合作伙伴工作负载中性能有所提升。IBM正在扩展其量子平台，将量子处理器与经典高性能计算资源集成，以应对更大工作负载、纠错研究和自动化量子工作流程。

欧盟拟推出量子法案，优先扶持本土供应商
11月9日，
据
The European Post披露欧盟《量子法案》草案内容，
草案将协调欧洲的量子研究、制造和商业化，同时通常将战略项目和公共采购权保留给欧盟控制的供应商和合格的国际合作伙伴。草案目标是到
2030年或不久后，每个系统约有100个错误更正逻辑量子比特，并提出量子计算、通信、传感和定时共享基础设施。该提案将对关键行业引入量子安全采购要求，资金依赖于未来的欧盟项目、国家贡献和私人投资。

# Weekly Report | QuEra, Harvard University, and Anthropic Research Shows AI Can Reduce Quantum Circuit Resource Requirements; IBM Announces Nighthawk r3, Plans 1,040-Qubit System for 2027…

## QuEra, Harvard University, and Anthropic Research Shows AI Can Reduce Quantum Circuit Resource Requirements

On November 10, researchers from QuEra, Harvard University, and Anthropic used Claude to design quantum circuits capable of reducing gate counts and qubit requirements across seven to eight computational building blocks. The research demonstrated a 12× reduction in Toffoli gates for Reed–Solomon decoders, a 9.9× reduction in total resources for Coulomb potential calculations, and a 39× reduction for fixed-point Gaussian functions. The team also developed a new reversible module inversion method that provides additional trade-offs between gate count and qubit requirements.

**Source:** https://www.quera.com/press-releases/harvard-anthropic-and-quera-breakthrough-research-uniquely-shows-ai-can-reduce-the-resources-quantum-applications-need-significantly-accelerating-the-era-of-useful-quantum-computing

## IBM Announces Nighthawk r3, Plans 1,040-Qubit System for 2027

On November 11, IBM announced the next-generation Quantum Nighthawk r3 processor, designed to execute 10,000 quantum operations on 520 programmable qubits, with plans to connect two processors into a 1,040-qubit system by 2027. The current Nighthawk r2 processor supports more than 7,500 quantum operations on 120 qubits and can achieve 100,000 samples per second; IBM reported performance improvements across multiple partner workloads. IBM is expanding its quantum platform to integrate quantum processors with classical high-performance computing resources to handle larger workloads, error correction research, and automated quantum workflows.

**Source:** https://newsroom.ibm.com/2026-11-11-ibm-quantum-nighthawk-demonstrates-new-levels-of-speed-and-quality,-with-plans-to-scale-beyond-1,000-qubits-in-2027

## EU Plans Quantum Act, Prioritizing Domestic Suppliers

On November 9, The European Post disclosed the contents of a draft EU Quantum Act. The draft would coordinate European quantum research, manufacturing, and commercialization, while generally reserving strategic projects and public procurement rights for EU-controlled suppliers and qualified international partners. The draft targets approximately 100 error-corrected logical qubits per system by 2030 or shortly thereafter, and proposes shared infrastructure for quantum computing, communications, sensing, and timing. The proposal would introduce quantum-safe procurement requirements for critical sectors, with funding dependent on future EU programs, national contributions, and private investment.

**Source:** https://theeuropeanpost.eu/policy-gazette/draft-quantum-act-could-bar-non-eu-suppliers-from-public-contracts/

## U.S. Commission on Quantum Primacy Releases Preliminary Report "Defining the American Quantum Era," Urging Sustained Investment

On November 10, the U.S. Commission on Quantum Primacy released its preliminary report, *Defining the American Quantum Era*, calling for the expansion of U.S. quantum leadership from research into deployment, manufacturing, and industrial scale. The report warned that China's public investment, manufacturing capabilities, and supply chains could enable it to scale quantum technologies faster than the United States. Priority areas include sustained research funding, coordinated hardware and software development, post-quantum security, foundry access, and workforce training, with implementation recommendations due by spring 2027.

- https://www.scsp.ai/defining-the-american-quantum-era/

## Q-Block Computing Announces Ottawa Headquarters, Expands Quantum Hardware R&D

On November 7, Canadian quantum systems developer Q-Block Computing announced the establishment of its corporate headquarters in Ottawa and the acquisition of an operational facility at 20 Colonnade Road. The expansion consolidates the company's research programs, optical and systems engineering, and administrative operations near federal defense and research agencies, while retaining existing manufacturing and assembly facilities in Alberta. The establishment of a permanent corporate headquarters reinforces the company's long-term commitment to developing quantum technologies in Canada.

**Source:** https://www.q-block.ca/archives/515

## TuringQ (图灵量子) Releases Four Application Scenarios for Gen3 Quantum Computer

On November 8, TuringQ (图灵量子) published four frontier application research results based on its third-generation photonic quantum computer, TuringQ Gen3, covering artificial intelligence, biopharmaceuticals, scientific computing, and financial technology. The four application research outcomes include quantum-assisted model optimization for large-model compression, quantum-enhanced protein design, quantum-prior scientific computing, and quantum sampling graph analysis. These results demonstrate new advances extending photonic quantum computing from core technological breakthroughs into application algorithm innovation, scenario validation, and industrial ecosystem collaboration.

## China's First Interconnectable Neutral-Atom Quantum Computer Prototype "Qianzhen" (乾阵) Unveiled in Hefei

On November 8, China's first interconnectable neutral-atom quantum computer prototype, "Qianzhen" (乾阵), was unveiled in Hefei, Anhui Province. The prototype was developed by Hefei Qianyuan Quantum Technology Co., Ltd. (合肥乾原量子科技有限公司, "Qianyuan Quantum"). Multi-machine interconnect capability was incorporated into the architecture from the outset, making it China's first neutral-atom quantum computer prototype with multi-system interconnect functionality. On the same day, the Shanxi University–Qianyuan Quantum Neutral-Atom Quantum Computing Joint Laboratory was inaugurated.

On November 9, Austrian semiconductor equipment manufacturer EV Group (EVG) announced that it will leverage its expertise in advanced packaging, heterogeneous integration, and photonic manufacturing to provide fabrication process support for quantum chip developers, helping quantum computing systems achieve scalable expansion. Its technologies encompass hybrid bonding, wafer bonding, nanoimprint lithography, and thin-wafer handling, and can meet chip integration requirements for superconducting quantum, photonic, spin, and ion trap quantum computing architectures, addressing challenges of high-density interconnects, heterogeneous material integration, and precision manufacturing encountered during qubit scaling.

The product portfolio includes PQC software libraries, FPGA, ASIC, and SoC cryptographic IP, cryptographic agility architectures, root-of-trust technology, and protection against side-channel and fault-injection attacks. ## Q.ANT and IONOS Launch Photonic Computing Pilot to Evaluate Photonic Computing Advantages

On November 9, Q.ANT and IONOS jointly launched a pilot project providing select developers with access to physical photonic processors via IONOS bare-metal servers hosted in Germany. Participants can run their own AI models and computational workloads on Q.ANT's second-generation Native Processing Unit (NPU) to evaluate performance on matrix multiplication and nonlinear mathematical function tasks. On November 9, Horizon Quantum and OQC announced the integration of OQC's 32-qubit superconducting quantum processor Toshiko with Horizon Quantum's Triple Alpha development environment, enabling pulse-level hardware control. The integration allows developers to characterize qubits, measure coherence parameters such as T1 and T2, and perform quantum gate calibration within the same environment used for quantum application development. The collaboration aims to provide developers with pulse-level control through Triple Alpha's programming environment and web-based API, simplifying hardware characterization and calibration workflows.

The investment supports Quanome's quantum life sciences strategy and provides it with an interest in QAI Labs' NOVA-3 platform, which combines AI-based antibody candidate selection, quantum algorithms running on classical simulators, and laboratory assays. The deployment uses Toshiba technology to exchange cryptographic keys between nodes and is integrating those keys with NIST post-quantum algorithms for quantum-safe message transmission. The platform operates in parallel with existing infrastructure, has hosted government evaluators and commercial prospective clients, and is the first in a planned series of deployments across multiple sites.

On November 9, Quantum X Labs announced the expansion of its AI-powered quantum error correction benchmarking to three IBM quantum processors: Fez, Kingston, and Pittsburgh. Experiments achieve an average state fidelity of 0.966 ± 0.0045, locking to arbitrary phase setpoints, continuous 24-hour active stabilization, and millisecond-scale phase switching, while suppressing crosstalk between reference pulses and the quantum channel. The scheme provides technical support for entanglement state characterization, fast feedforward, and photonic quantum information processing in fiber quantum networks. The results were published on November 12 in *Physical Review Applied*.

**Source:** https://journals.aps.org/prapplied/abstract/10.1103/ftlp-j83g

## NIST and Collaborators Study High-Precision Graphene Quantum Hall Array Resistance Standards Based on Star–Delta Transformations

This research applies star–delta network transformations to reduce the number of Hall bars required in high-resistance graphene quantum Hall arrays, presenting array designs targeting approximately 1, 10, and 100 MΩ, and proposing a multi-arm programmable scheme. Three isomorphic devices each containing 28 Hall bars are measured; at 1.6 K, two devices achieve quantized resistance of approximately 1 MΩ at 5 and 6 T, respectively, with relative deviations within 80 parts per billion. Measurements are performed using three-terminal connections, dual-source bridges, and substitution methods without requiring a cryogenic current comparator, demonstrating a helium-free high-resistance quantum resistance calibration approach that shortens the traceability chain for industrial calibration. The results were published on November 9 in *npj 2D Materials and Applications*.

## Nanjing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics and Collaborators Study Unified Control of Intrinsic Nonlinear Spin Dynamics

## University of Texas at Austin and Collaborators Measure Single-Mode Vacuum Squeezing in a SNAIL Parametric Amplifier

This research measures single-mode vacuum squeezing generated by a SNAIL (Superconducting Nonlinear Asymmetric Inductive eLement) parametric amplifier under near-practical-application conditions, examining the effect of Kerr nonlinearity by varying the applied magnetic flux and pump power. Results show that at a fixed squeezing frequency, an approximately twofold variation in Kerr nonlinearity does not produce a significant change in achievable squeezing; theoretical modeling confirms that internal resonator loss and microwave chain insertion loss are the dominant limiting factors. The study identifies loss reduction as the key to improving practical squeezing performance in such devices. The results were published on November 10 in *Physical Review Applied*.

## University of Oxford and Collaborators Study Passive Imaging with Quantum Advantage

This research proposes and implements a Fourier-domain partitioning method: incident light is optically preprocessed before detection, with the Fourier plane divided into regions detected independently and subsequently reconstructed via post-processing. Fisher information analysis demonstrates that this method outperforms direct imaging for high-spatial-frequency components, reducing the number of photons required to achieve a given signal-to-noise ratio and improving resolution in photon-starved regimes. In microscopy experiments, Fisher information for high-spatial-frequency components is enhanced fivefold. The method is passive and applicable to microscopy, astronomy, and remote sensing scenarios where active illumination is not feasible, providing a general strategy for quantum-optimized super-resolution imaging. The results were published on November 11 in *Science Advances*.

## Universidad Carlos III de Madrid Analyzes Quantum Metrological Advantages of Higher-Order Squeezed States

This research analyzes two classes of non-Gaussian states — higher-order phase states and multiphoton squeezed states — in standard interferometric or rotation parameter estimation, comparing them with optimal Gaussian squeezed vacuum states at equal mean occupation numbers. Results show that both classes can provide higher quantum Fisher information under certain conditions, with advantages exhibiting different characteristics in low- and high-occupation-number regimes depending on the specific state family. Increasing the squeezing order can enhance the metrological advantage, but fully exploiting this advantage requires measurement of higher-order observables. The results further examine pure dephasing and zero-temperature damping, finding the states to be relatively robust against moderate damping but sensitive to pure dephasing, delineating the potential and practical limitations of non-Gaussian resources for improving measurement precision. The results were published on November 12 in *Physical Review Research*.

## Russian Academy of Sciences and Collaborators Study Giant Nonlinearity of Kinetic Inductance in Superconducting Composite Strips

This research observes an approximately 50-fold variation of kinetic inductance with current in NbN/Al (niobium nitride/aluminum) superconducting composite strips, significantly exceeding the typical variation of only a few tens of percent found in ordinary superconductors. The effect is associated with proximity-effect-induced superconductivity in the aluminum layer: under specific parameters, the superconducting current as a function of Cooper pair momentum exhibits a plateau well below the depairing current, causing the corresponding differential kinetic inductance to increase sharply. The study demonstrates a pathway for enhancing current-response nonlinearity through superconducting composite structures, providing a basis for device design of highly sensitive electromagnetic radiation detectors, calorimeters, parametric amplifiers, and magnetometers. ## University of Chicago and Collaborators Extract Information from Superradiant Pulses Using Simple Measurements

This research investigates how to extract phase information encoded in the initial spin state from superradiant photon pulses generated by a spin ensemble. Addressing the challenge that the light field produced by superradiance is in a complex non-classical state making information extraction difficult, the study proposes a homodyne measurement scheme combining optimized filters and linear estimators. Theoretical analysis shows that this method can recover the scaling of quantum Fisher information of the initial spin state with spin number N, including N²-Heisenberg scaling in some cases. The study also finds that in the large-spin-ensemble limit, the temporal mode carrying optimal phase information contains only a small fraction of the total emitted photons, suggesting that phase information may be concentrated in specific field modes. The results were published on November 12 in *PRX Quantum*.

## University of Landau (Germany) Studies Bound States in the Continuum Formed by Quantum Interference in Ultracold Atom Collisions

This research uses Floquet control to coherently couple two tunable Feshbach resonances in ultracold lithium-6 atom collisions, causing the amplitudes leading to the same scattering continuum to destructively interfere. At critical parameters, both elastic and inelastic couplings between the molecular state and the continuum vanish simultaneously; the molecular state remains localized despite lying above the dissociation threshold. In the experiment, resonant scattering features disappear, and colliding atoms scatter from each other negligibly. Full coupled-channel calculations and a minimal non-Hermitian model quantitatively reproduce the experimental results, confirming the state as a Friedrich–Wintgen bound state in the continuum, providing a pathway for controlling the coupling of quantum matter to its environment and constructing non-Hermitian Hamiltonians. The results were published on November 9 in *Nature Physics*.

## Beijing Normal University and Collaborators Explore Deconfined Quantum Critical Points in Dissipative Spin-1/2 Chains

This research studies spin-1/2 J–Q₃ chains coupled to independent bosonic baths using non-Abelian bosonization, renormalization group methods, and quantum Monte Carlo simulations to map out the phase diagram and characterize phase transitions. Strong dissipation is found to stabilize the antiferromagnetic phase in sub-Ohmic, Ohmic, and super-Ohmic baths; continuous antiferromagnet–valence-bond-solid phase transitions emerge with increasing multi-spin interactions in the sub-Ohmic and Ohmic regimes. The Ohmic critical point exhibits spinon deconfinement and emergent O(4) symmetry; sub-Ohmic transitions are governed by a continuous family of fixed points parameterized by the bath spectral exponent s. An antiferromagnet-to-quasi-long-range-ordered phase transition is also proposed in the super-Ohmic regime. The results were published on November 9 in *Physical Review Letters*.

## University of Cologne Studies Local Operator Entanglement Page Curves from Free Probability Theory

This research uses free probability theory to analytically compute the asymptotic values of local operator entanglement for arbitrary Rényi indices under Haar-random dynamics. Results show that for traceless operators, the first two orders of the large-dimension expansion coincide exactly with the Page curve of random quantum states; the leading term of local operator entanglement is independent of the initial operator, while higher-order operator correlations are reflected in finite-size corrections. The study further indicates that in chaotic systems at long times, local operator entanglement depends only on part of the correlation structure described by the eigenstate thermalization hypothesis, providing a theoretical basis for distinguishing classical simulability of operators from higher-order information scrambling. The results were published on November 10 in *Physical Review Letters*.

## Palacký University Olomouc and Collaborators Estimate Adaptive Entanglement Negativity Based on Collective Measurements

This research addresses the challenge of large measurement resource requirements for quantitative entanglement characterization in two-qubit and qubit–qutrit systems, proposing an adaptive estimation method combining two-copy collective measurements with machine learning. The study uses long short-term memory (LSTM) networks to sequentially process measurement outcomes, dynamically selecting the next measurement setting based on results obtained so far while simultaneously estimating entanglement negativity. Numerical studies show that with a limited number of measurement settings, the adaptive strategy can estimate entanglement more accurately than non-adaptive approaches with pre-fixed settings, providing a pathway for reducing measurement overhead in quantum state entanglement characterization. ## Durham University and Collaborators Study Topological Edge States in a Synthetic Molecular Dimension

This research uses the rotational states of ultracold RbCs molecules to construct a one-dimensional synthetic lattice and study the topological properties of the Su–Schrieffer–Heeger (SSH) model. Spectroscopic probing is performed via auxiliary rotational states, and time dynamics following deterministic state preparation are studied. Long coherence times of approximately 500 tunneling periods are achieved even when the lattice spans eight rotational states. Using full-site-resolved readout after long evolution times, the researchers study the robustness of topologically protected edge states against perturbations that preserve or break chiral symmetry. This work establishes ultracold molecules as a powerful platform for quantum simulation in synthetic dimensions. The results were published on November 11 in *Nature Communications*.

## Freie Universität Berlin Studies Optimal Learning of Quantum Channels in Diamond Distance

This research proposes a tomography algorithm based on the Choi-state representation of channels, reducing channel learning to pure-state tomography, and proves that the number of queries required for any fixed constant precision achieves optimal dependence on input dimension, output dimension, and Kraus rank. Dimension-dependent lower bounds matching the algorithm are also established, determining the query complexity in this regime. The framework unifies tomography of quantum states, unitary operations, and measurements into a single description, providing an information-theoretic resource benchmark for calibration, verification, and noise process characterization of quantum devices. ## ETH Zurich Studies Hilbert Space Fragmentation Induced by Generalized Symmetries

This research proves that generalized symmetries — including higher-form symmetries, subsystem symmetries, and gauge symmetries — can themselves produce exponentially many symmetry sectors in a tensor-product basis, while non-invertible symmetries can further induce fragmentation within individual symmetry sectors. The study shows that fragmentation in several known models can be attributed to these symmetries, implying that exponential growth of Krylov subspaces alone cannot determine ergodicity breaking. The research further shows that thermalization restricted to Krylov subspaces can produce disorder-free localization when subspaces lack translation invariance, providing new theoretical explanations for thermalization and localization in constrained quantum many-body systems. The results were published on November 12 in *Physical Review Letters*.

## National Institute of Science Education and Research (NISER), India and Collaborators Study Physical Interpretation of Liouvillian Operator Eigenmodes

This research combines left and right eigenstates to construct gauge-invariant quasi-probability measures, interpreting eigenmodes as a set of coherences and visualizing them in a doubled phase space. Results show that under a wide range of linear and nonlinear dissipation conditions, damped oscillators retain quantized orbits with measurable characteristics; thermal baths broaden the orbits and cause characteristic multi-stage relaxation. ## University of Science and Technology of China (USTC) and Collaborators Extract Pairing Gaps from van Hove Singularities in RF Spectra of the Fermi–Hubbard Model

This research proposes extracting pairing gaps from van Hove singularities in the radio-frequency (RF) spectrum of the three-dimensional attractive Fermi–Hubbard model. Four types of singularities are classified and analyzed; it is proven that their spectral positions depend on the pairing gap and chemical potential through simple algebraic relations, so that measuring two clearly distinguishable singularities suffices to simultaneously determine both parameters without fitting the full spectrum. Numerical simulations including lifetime and scattering broadening show that these features remain visible in momentum-integrated spectra and longitudinal-momentum-integrated spectra; in the strong-coupling regime where conventional band-back-bending analysis loses sensitivity, the singularity features become more pronounced. At half-filling, particle–hole symmetry fixes the chemical potential, so that only one singularity needs to be measured to extract the gap, providing a spectroscopic method for pairing diagnostics in quantum-simulated Fermi systems. The results were published on November 12 in *Physical Review Research*.

**Source:** https://journals.aps.org/prresearch/abstract/10.1103/mthq-q8kh

## Hebrew University of Jerusalem and Collaborators Study Quantum Transport in Disordered Spin Networks

This research uses a two-dimensional tight-binding model incorporating dipolar interactions and local dephasing to study transport and relaxation when spin impurities couple to small spatially disordered spin networks. Results show that geometric inhomogeneity can produce hierarchical coupling, causing local cluster equilibration and global equilibration to occur on significantly different timescales. A minimal three-site model reveals that effective detuning formed by strong internal hybridization suppresses transfer to weakly coupled sites, leading to greatly prolonged relaxation times under weak dephasing. Non-equilibrium steady-state calculations and simulations over multiple disorder realizations verify this mechanism, also showing that dephasing can modulate competing transport pathways. The study demonstrates that network geometry and connectivity structure are important factors determining the dynamics of small spin baths. The results were published on November 12 in *Physical Review Research*.

**Source:** https://journals.aps.org/prresearch/abstract/10.1103/znwb-71hy
